pages.c01-p01: Describe networks by their scope: local area network (LAN), metropolitan area network (MAN) and wide area network (WAN)
pages.c01-p02: Describe the purpose of the network resources: network card, server, switched hub, repeater, wireless access point, media converter, IP address and media access control (MAC) address
pages.c01-p03: Define the purpose of an IP address and a MAC address
pages.c01-p04: Describe the features of a peer-to-peer (P2P) and server-based networks
pages.c01-p05: Evaluate the bus, star and ring network topologies

q.q: In networking, what is meant by a node?
o: A computer or other device linked to the network
The point where a LAN joins the internet
A packet of data travelling between devices
The central cable that all devices attach to
q.why: A node is any computer or device connected to the network; the central cable is the backbone.

q.q: CCEA describes networks by their scope. Which three things does scope cover?
o: The bandwidth, the latency and the error rate
The topology, the protocol and the number of servers
The area covered, how links are made and who it is for
The number of nodes, switches and access points
q.why: Scope is the size of the area, the technology of the links and the purpose (who the network serves).

q.q: Which network scope best describes fibre links joining a city council's offices spread across one city?
o: WAN
MAN
PAN
LAN
q.why: A metropolitan area network covers a city or large town, typically with fibre or wireless links.

q.q: Which network scope covers one building or a group of buildings close together on one site?
o: WAN
LAN
MAN
PAN
q.why: A local area network serves one site and is owned by one organisation.

q.q: Which of these is the largest wide area network?
o: A city's public Wi-Fi network
A university's campus network
A bank's head office network
The internet
q.why: The notes describe the internet as the largest WAN; a city's public Wi-Fi is a MAN.

q.q: Which communication links are most typical of a WAN?
o: Undersea fibre cables and communication satellites
Copper Ethernet cable owned by the organisation
Fibre optic cable laid across one city
Wi-Fi access points throughout one building
q.why: WANs span countries using telecommunication links rented from providers, such as undersea cables and satellites.

q.q: What most clearly distinguishes a LAN from a WAN?
o: A LAN always uses wireless links rather than cables
A WAN never uses fibre optic cable for its links
A LAN covers one site and its links are owned by the organisation
A LAN cannot share printers or files between its users
q.why: Area covered and ownership of the links are the clearest differences; LANs share printers and often use cable.

q.q: Why does an organisation running a WAN usually pay a telecommunications company?
o: Its switched hubs must be serviced by the provider
It must buy a separate IP address for every node
Its links cross land it does not own, so it rents them
Its nodes are too close together to cable directly
q.why: A WAN crosses land the organisation does not own, so it rents the links.

q.q: A company controls the speed and security of its own network because it owns all the cables, switches and access points. Which scope is this most likely to be?
o: The internet
LAN
WAN
MAN
q.why: A LAN's equipment belongs to the organisation, so it controls speed and security.

q.q: Compared with a LAN, why is data on a WAN more exposed?
o: It passes through other parties' equipment on the way
It is always sent without any form of addressing
It travels as radio signals that anyone can receive
It is stored on every node it passes through
q.why: Long WAN links pass through equipment owned by other parties, so the data is more exposed.

q.q: Which statement about speed and errors is correct?
o: WAN links are faster than LAN links because they use fibre throughout
Short LAN links are fast with few errors; WAN links have more latency
LAN links have more latency because they carry more users
MAN links have fewer errors than LAN links because they are longer
q.why: Short LAN links are fast with few errors, while long WAN links have more delay (latency) and cost more per megabit.

q.q: A university joins its campuses across a large town with fibre optic links. Which scope is this?
o: MAN
WAN
LAN
PAN
q.why: A university's campuses across a city or large town is given in the notes as a MAN example.

q.q: A bank links its branches across several countries. Which scope of network is this?
o: WAN
LAN
PAN
MAN
q.why: A WAN connects sites that are far apart, such as a bank and its branches.

q.q: One person's phone, earbuds and smartwatch are linked by Bluetooth over a few metres. What is this called, and is it in the A2 1 specification?
o: A PAN; it replaces the MAN in the specification
A LAN; it is one of the three scopes in the specification
A MAN; it is one of the three scopes in the specification
A PAN; it is not one of the scopes in the specification
q.why: A personal area network is mentioned for interest only; the three scopes to know are LAN, MAN and WAN.

q.q: An exam table asks for a scope and a different communication medium for each of a LAN, MAN and WAN. Which set of answers is best?
o: LAN Ethernet cable; MAN fibre optic; WAN communication satellites
LAN Wi-Fi; MAN Wi-Fi; WAN undersea cables
LAN communication satellites; MAN Ethernet cable; WAN fibre optic
LAN fibre optic; MAN Ethernet cable; WAN Wi-Fi hotspot
q.why: The notes suggest Ethernet for a LAN, fibre for a MAN and satellites for a WAN, with no answer repeated.

q.q: Which purpose matches a MAN?
o: Linking one person's devices over a few metres
Connecting sites in different countries
Serving the community and organisations within one city
Serving one organisation on a single site
q.why: A MAN serves the people and organisations of a city or large town.

q.q: What is the purpose of a network interface card (NIC)?
o: To regenerate weak signals over a long cable run
To share files and printers with the other nodes
To join a fibre optic cable to a copper cable
To connect a computer to the network so it can communicate
q.why: The NIC connects the computer to the network; sharing resources is the server's job.

q.q: Which address is carried on a network card?
o: The MAC address
The port address
The IP address
The DNS address
q.why: The MAC address is burned into the NIC when it is made.

q.q: Where is a network card usually found in a modern computer?
o: Attached to the end of the backbone
Built into the motherboard
Inside the wireless access point
Plugged into the switched hub
q.why: Most network cards are now built into the motherboard.

q.q: Which resource regenerates a signal that has weakened over a long cable?
o: Network card
Switched hub
Repeater
Media converter
q.why: A repeater re-creates and amplifies attenuated signals.

q.q: What is attenuation?
o: The copying of a packet to every port on a hub
The weakening of a signal as it travels along a cable
The collision of two packets sent at the same time
The change of a signal from light to electricity
q.why: Signals weaken (attenuate) and distort over long runs, which is why repeaters are used.

q.q: Which statement about a repeater is correct?
o: It checks each packet for errors before passing it on
It stores packets until the destination node is free
It reads the destination address and forwards selectively
It regenerates the signal but does not store or check the data
q.why: The notes stress that a repeater simply regenerates the signal; it does not store or check data.

q.q: Which resource joins a fibre optic cable to a copper cable?
o: Wireless access point
Media converter
Switched hub
Repeater
q.why: A media converter changes the physical signal between dissimilar media.

q.q: What does a media converter actually change?
o: The IP address of each packet into a MAC address
The physical signal, for example light into electrical signals
The data in each packet into an encrypted form
The speed of the network to match the slowest node
q.why: It converts the physical signal from one medium to another, e.g. light in fibre to electrical signals in copper.

q.q: What does a switched hub do with a packet it receives?
o: Sends it to every node so the right one can pick it up
Reads its destination address and forwards it only to that node
Regenerates it and passes it on to the next segment
Stores it until the server is free to process it
q.why: Unlike an old unswitched hub, a switched hub forwards each packet only to its destination.

q.q: What did an old-style unswitched hub do that a switched hub does not?
o: Changed light signals into electrical signals
Forwarded each packet only to its destination
Copied every packet to every port
Joined the LAN to the internet
q.why: An unswitched hub copied every packet to every port, so nodes shared bandwidth and packets collided.

q.q: Why does a switched hub improve performance compared with an unswitched hub?
o: It converts all traffic to fibre optic, which is faster
Several conversations can happen at once without packets colliding
It gives every node its own IP address from a pool
It boosts the signal so data travels further along each cable
q.why: Sending each packet only to its destination lets several conversations take place at once.

q.q: Many switched hubs load-balance. What does this mean?
o: Spreading print jobs evenly across the network printers
Sharing the processing load between all the client computers
Sending traffic along different network segments when one is busy
Giving each node an equal share of the server's storage
q.why: Load-balancing in a switched hub sends traffic along a different segment when one is busy.

q.q: CCEA uses the term switched hub for which device?
o: What is usually called a repeater
What is usually called a modem
What is usually called a switch
What is usually called a router
q.why: CCEA's switched hub is what is commonly called a switch.

q.q: How does a router differ from a switched hub?
o: A router works within one network; a switched hub works between networks
A router works between networks; a switched hub works within one
A router regenerates signals; a switched hub converts media
A router has no address; a switched hub uses IP addresses
q.why: A router joins networks, e.g. the school LAN to the internet; a switched hub connects nodes within a LAN.

q.q: What is the purpose of a wireless access point (WAP)?
o: To join two networks that use different cable types
To let Wi-Fi devices join a wired network by radio
To give each wireless device a fixed MAC address
To regenerate signals over a long wireless link
q.why: A WAP uses radio transmitters and antennae to let wireless devices join the wired network.

q.q: What is the area covered by a wireless access point called?
o: A segment
A domain
A backbone
A hotspot
q.why: The area a WAP covers is a hotspot, e.g. an open-plan office or café.

q.q: A WAP usually connects on to which other device?
o: A repeater
A media converter
A terminator
A router
q.why: The notes say a WAP usually connects on to a router.

q.q: What is the purpose of a server on a network?
o: To regenerate signals that have weakened
To manage and share resources for the rest of the network
To connect each computer to the network cable
To forward each packet to its destination port
q.why: A server manages and shares resources and handles requests from other nodes.

q.q: Which description fits a print server?
o: It converts print data from fibre to copper cable
It regenerates the signals sent to remote printers
It gives each network printer its own MAC address
It queues and spools the print jobs for shared printers
q.why: A print server queues and spools jobs for the network's printers.

q.q: Which type of server stores users' files and controls access to them?
o: File server
Proxy server
Print server
Mail server
q.why: A file server stores users' files and controls who can access them.

q.q: A hotel has guest rooms 150 m from its office, too far for an ordinary cable signal. Which resource should be added part-way along the cable?
o: Media converter
Network card
Wireless access point
Repeater
q.why: A repeater regenerates the weakened signal so data can travel further.

q.q: A café wants customers' phones and laptops to use its network without cables. Which resource is needed?
o: Repeater
File server
Media converter
Wireless access point
q.why: A WAP creates a hotspot so wireless devices can join the network.

q.q: A school's fibre optic link from another building arrives at a room cabled with copper Ethernet. Which device joins them?
o: Media converter
Repeater
Wireless access point
Router
q.why: The media converter joins dissimilar media by changing light to electrical signals.

q.q: Which list contains only types of server named in the notes?
o: File, print, web, mail, DNS and proxy
File, print, web, mail, DNS and repeater
File, print, hotspot, mail, DNS and proxy
File, print, web, mail, switch and proxy
q.why: The notes list file, print, web, mail, DNS and proxy servers; repeaters, hotspots and switches are not servers.

q.q: A pupil writes: "A switched hub sends data to every computer on the network." What is wrong with this?
o: That describes a router; a switched hub only connects two networks together
That describes a repeater; a switched hub only regenerates weak signals
That describes an old unswitched hub; a switched hub forwards only to the destination
Nothing; a switched hub broadcasts every packet to every node
q.why: The notes warn against this error: sending to every node was the old unswitched hub.

q.q: What does an IP address identify?
o: The make and model of the device on the network
The physical network card, fixed by its manufacturer
The cable socket on the switched hub the device uses
A device's connection on a network, so data can be delivered to it
q.why: An IP address identifies the device's connection; the MAC address identifies the physical card.

q.q: Who sets a device's MAC address?
o: The DHCP server
The manufacturer of the network card
The internet service provider
The network administrator
q.why: The MAC address is coded onto the NIC when it is made.

q.q: How many bits are there in an IPv4 address?
q.why: IPv4 is 32 bits; MAC addresses are 48 bits and IPv6 is 128 bits.

q.q: How many bits are there in a MAC address?
q.why: A MAC address is 48 bits, written as six pairs of hexadecimal digits.

q.q: Which is a valid IPv4 address?
q.why: An IPv4 address is four denary octets each 0 to 255; 300 is out of range and the third option is a MAC address.

q.q: Which is written in the correct format for a MAC address?
q.why: A MAC address is six pairs of hex digits separated by colons; g is not a hex digit and five pairs is only 40 bits.

q.q: A laptop is taken from school to home and connected there. Which address changes?
o: Its MAC address only
Both its IP and MAC addresses
Its IP address only
Neither address changes
q.why: The IP address reflects where the device connects; the MAC address is fixed to the card.

q.q: Which kind of IP address is lent to a device each time it connects, from a shared pool?
o: Static IP address
Dynamic IP address
MAC IP address
Physical IP address
q.why: Dynamic addresses are handed out from a pool by a DHCP server and may differ next time.

q.q: Which server hands out dynamic IP addresses?
o: DNS server
File server
DHCP server
Proxy server
q.why: A DHCP server lends addresses from a pool; a DNS server is a different type of server.

q.q: Why would a network printer usually be given a static IP address?
o: So its MAC address can be changed when it moves
So it does not need a network card to connect
So it receives a new address from the pool each day
So other devices can always find it at the same address
q.why: Static addresses are permanent and set by hand, useful for servers and printers that others must always find.

q.q: Which device uses MAC addresses to deliver data to the right port within a local network?
o: Switched hub
Repeater
Media converter
Router
q.why: Switched hubs use MAC addresses within a LAN; routers use IP addresses between networks.

q.q: Which device uses IP addresses to forward packets between networks?
o: Router
Wireless access point
Repeater
Switched hub
q.why: Routers forward packets between networks using IP addresses.

q.q: What is MAC filtering?
o: A WAP hiding its MAC address from nearby devices
A router accepting only devices whose MAC addresses are on a list
A server changing the MAC address of unknown devices
A switched hub blocking packets that have no IP address
q.why: MAC filtering admits only listed MAC addresses, controlling which devices may join a wireless network.

q.q: Why is a MAC address useful for tracking a device even when its IP address changes?
o: The MAC address is fixed for the life of the card
The MAC address contains the device's location
The MAC address is reissued by the ISP each day
The MAC address is longer, so it holds more data
q.why: Because it does not change, the MAC address still identifies the device when its dynamic IP address changes.

q.q: Which analogy for the two addresses is used in the notes?
o: IP address is like a house key; MAC address is like a postcode
IP address is like a passport number; MAC address is like a postal address
IP address is like a phone number; MAC address is like a surname
IP address is like a postal address; MAC address is like a passport number
q.why: The IP address depends on where you are, like a postal address; the MAC address stays with you, like a passport number.

q.q: Who sets a device's public IP address?
o: The user, when the device is first set up
The manufacturer of its network card
The switched hub it is plugged into
Its internet service provider
q.why: The public IP address is set by the ISP and reflects where the device is connected.

q.q: Approximately how many addresses do IPv4's 32 bits give?
o: About 65 thousand
About 16.7 million
About 281 trillion
About 4.3 billion
q.why: 2 to the power 32 is about 4.3 billion, and these have run out.

q.q: Which is the best way to distinguish a MAC address from an IP address?
o: The MAC address is set by the ISP; the IP address is set by the manufacturer
The MAC address identifies the physical NIC on the LAN; the IP address identifies the device's connection
The MAC address identifies the device's connection; the IP address identifies the physical NIC
The MAC address is 32 bits; the IP address is 48 bits
q.why: A distinguish answer needs a matched pair: what each address identifies.

q.q: Each part of an IPv4 address is an octet. What range of denary values can each octet hold?
q.why: An octet is 8 bits, so it holds 0 to 255.

q.q: How is a MAC address normally written?
o: Eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons
Six denary numbers from 0 to 99 separated by dots
Four denary numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots
Six two-digit hexadecimal numbers separated by colons
q.why: A MAC address is 48 bits shown as six hex pairs; the dotted denary form is IPv4.

q.q: What is the main feature of a server-based network?
o: At least one dedicated server controls resources for client computers
Each user decides what is shared from their own machine
All computers are joined in a loop and pass a token
Every computer has equal status and shares its own resources
q.why: A server-based network has at least one dedicated server; the others are clients.

q.q: Which is a feature of a peer-to-peer network?
o: Backup is carried out centrally on one machine
Each computer both supplies and uses resources
A dedicated file server stores all users' files
Users log on to the server at any client
q.why: Every peer is both a supplier and a consumer of resources.

q.q: In a server-based network, what are the other computers called?
o: Terminators
Peers
Clients
Hosts
q.why: The other computers are clients: they request resources and the server supplies them.

q.q: What does dedicated mean when describing a server?
o: It is connected directly to the internet
It is reserved for the network manager only
It does nothing but serve the network
It belongs to one particular user
q.why: A dedicated server does nothing but serve the network.

q.q: Which of these does the server control in a server-based network?
o: Only the cabling and the switched hub
Only the printers, while each user controls their own files
Only internet access, while peers share files directly
File storage and backup, software, printers and security
q.why: The server controls file storage and backup, application software, printers and security.

q.q: What is the main security advantage of a server-based network?
o: Data never leaves the client computers
No usernames or passwords are needed
It has no single point of failure
Log-ons and access rights are managed centrally
q.why: The server controls who can log on and what they can reach.

q.q: Which situation suits a peer-to-peer network best?
o: Three PCs in a home office sharing a printer
A hospital with two thousand users
A bank with branches in many towns
A university with several campuses
q.why: P2P suits a handful of users with low-risk data.

q.q: Why is security weak on a peer-to-peer network?
o: All data is sent to every node on the backbone
The server stores all passwords in one unprotected file
Shares are set separately on each machine by its user
Every user must know the server's administrator password
q.why: There is no central control: each user decides what is shared on their own machine.

q.q: On a peer-to-peer network, who is responsible for backup?
o: The network manager backs up each peer overnight
Each user must back up their own machine
The internet service provider backs up shared files
The server backs up all machines centrally
q.why: With no dedicated server, there is no central backup.

q.q: What happens on a server-based network if the server fails?
o: The clients lose the services the server provides
The clients take over as peers automatically
Nothing, as each client keeps a full copy of the data
Only the node with the faulty cable is affected
q.why: The server is a single point of failure for the services it provides.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of a peer-to-peer network for performance?
o: Every packet must pass through a central hub
Users must wait for the token before logging on
The server becomes a bottleneck when overloaded
A peer slows down when others use its resources
q.why: On P2P each peer is also used by others, so it slows down; a bottleneck server applies to server-based networks.

q.q: Why is a server-based network more expensive to set up than a peer-to-peer network?
o: It needs server hardware, server software and a network manager
It needs a wireless access point for every client
It needs every client computer to be replaced each year
It needs a separate cable from every client to every other client
q.why: The notes list server hardware, server software and a network manager as the costs.

q.q: Which reason explains why usernames and passwords on a server-based network help security?
o: They encrypt every file stored on the client computers
Only authorised users can log on, and attempts are logged
They let each user decide what to share from their PC
They stop the server from failing when overloaded
q.why: Only users with valid credentials can log on, and the server logs log-ons and failed attempts.

q.q: What can a network administrator do because accounts are managed centrally?
o: Set access rights, force password changes and disable leavers' accounts
Change each client's MAC address to match its user
Let each user set their own access rights on their PC
Remove the need for passwords on trusted clients
q.why: Central management lets the administrator set rights, force password changes and disable accounts.

q.q: A user logs on at a different client from usual on a server-based network. What happens?
o: They can only see files stored on that particular client
They must create a new account on that client first
They still get their own storage area, printers and software
They lose access to the printers until they return
q.why: Users can log on at any client and get their own storage area and allowed resources.

q.q: Which four points best describe the features of a P2P network?
o: Equal status; token passing; one-way data; no collisions
No dedicated server; equal status; each supplies resources; each consumes resources
Dedicated server; central backup; central security; users log on
No dedicated server; cheap; easy to set up; uses existing PCs
q.why: The exam tip lists these four features; cost points are advantages, not features.

q.q: Which is an example of peer-to-peer networking given in the notes?
o: A school's network with a file server
A council's fibre network across a city
File-sharing applications on the internet
A bank's network of branches
q.why: The notes give a small office sharing a printer and internet file-sharing applications as P2P examples.

q.q: A law firm with 60 staff stores sensitive client records. Which network model should it choose and why?
o: Peer-to-peer, because there is no single point of failure
Peer-to-peer, because it is cheap and simple to set up
Server-based, because it needs no network manager
Server-based, for central security, access rights and backup
q.why: Many users and sensitive data need central control of security and backup.

q.q: What is a network topology?
o: The set of rules for sending data on a network
The layout of the nodes and the links between them
The way resources are controlled on a network
The size of the area that a network covers
q.why: Topology is the layout; scope is the area covered and the model is how resources are controlled.

q.q: In a bus topology, what is the main cable that every node is attached to called?
o: The backbone
The token
The hotspot
The ring
q.why: Every node on a bus is attached to one main cable, the backbone.

q.q: What is fitted at each end of a bus backbone?
o: A token
A media converter
A repeater
A terminator
q.why: Terminators stop the signal reflecting back along the cable.

q.q: What is the purpose of a terminator on a bus network?
o: To stop signals reflecting back along the backbone
To pass the token from one end to the other
To convert the signal from copper to fibre
To boost signals that have weakened along the backbone
q.why: Terminators absorb the signal at each end so it does not reflect.

q.q: How does a ring network avoid collisions?
o: The hub queues packets until the cable is free
Terminators absorb the signal at each end
Only the node holding the token may transmit
Data travels in both directions at once
q.why: Token passing means only one node sends at a time.

q.q: In which direction does data travel round a ring network?
o: Both directions along the loop
To every node at the same time
One direction only, node to node
Directly to the destination through a central hub
q.why: Data travels node to node in one direction until it reaches its destination.

q.q: Which method does a bus network use to deal with collisions?
o: MAC filtering
CSMA/CD
Load-balancing
Token passing
q.why: A bus uses CSMA/CD: check if the backbone is busy, wait, and resend after a collision.

q.q: Which topology isolates a cable fault to a single node?
o: Star
Ring
All three equally
Bus
q.why: In a star each node has its own cable to the hub, so a cable fault affects only that node.

q.q: Why is a star network the most secure of the three topologies?
o: Data travels round it in one direction only
It encrypts every packet as it leaves the hub
It uses no cables so data cannot be tapped
The hub sends each packet only to its recipient
q.why: On a bus or ring, data passes other nodes; in a star the hub sends it only to the recipient.

q.q: What happens in a star network if the central hub fails?
o: Only the node nearest the hub is affected
Data continues along the backbone
The whole network stops
The nodes pass a token round instead
q.why: All communication goes through the centre, so its failure stops the whole network.

q.q: Why does performance on a bus network fall as more nodes are added?
o: Each node must regenerate the signal for the next one
The central hub runs out of free ports for the cables
More traffic leads to more collisions on the shared backbone
Each extra node must wait longer for the token to arrive
q.why: All nodes share one backbone, so more nodes means more traffic and collisions.

q.q: Why is adding a node to a ring network difficult?
o: The hub must be replaced with one that has more ports
The ring must be cut and rejoined, disrupting the network
A new terminator must be fitted at each end of the cable
The new node must be given the token permanently
q.why: Adding a node means cutting the ring and joining the new node to both ends.

q.q: Which topology makes adding a node easiest, with no disruption?
o: Bus, as the backbone needs no terminators
Bus, as each new node reduces collisions
Ring, as the token adapts to the new node
Star, by running a cable to a free hub port
q.why: In a star you simply connect another cable to a free port.

q.q: Why might repeaters be fitted on a long ring network?
o: To absorb the signal when it returns to the sender
To stop the token travelling in the wrong direction
To send each packet only to its destination
To boost the signal, which weakens over a long ring
q.why: Over a long ring the signal weakens, so repeaters boost it.

q.q: Which topology uses the least cable?
o: Star
Star with a switched hub
Bus
Ring
q.why: A bus uses one shared backbone, so it needs the least cable; a star needs the most.

q.q: Why is there no contention for cables in a star network?
o: Data travels in one direction only
The token allows one sender at a time
Terminators remove old signals
No two nodes share a cable
q.why: Every node has its own cable to the centre, so there is no contention.

q.q: On a bus, a drop cable to one node breaks. What is the effect?
o: The whole network stops
All nodes beyond the break are cut off
Only that node is affected
The token is lost and must be regenerated
q.why: A drop cable affects only its own node; a break in the backbone stops everything.

q.q: Which statement correctly evaluates the ring topology for performance?
o: Unpredictable, because nodes transmit whenever they want
Falls steadily as traffic and collisions grow
Predictable, with no collisions, but data must pass every node
High, because no two nodes ever share a cable
q.why: Token passing gives predictable performance without collisions, but data passes other nodes on the way.

q.q: A school asks which topology would be affected least by a single cable failure. Which judgement is best justified?
o: Star, because a failed cable cuts off only the node on that cable
Bus, because a broken backbone still lets nodes send to each other
Ring, because the token is never lost when a cable breaks
Ring, because data can always go the other way round the loop
